 He Jumps on the Harley-Davidson Bandwagon at 70. His New Motorcycle Loan Can’t Be Denied Just Because He Collects Social Security
 A 70-year-old with a $3,000 Social Security check and his eye on a new Harley walks up to the financing desk. Federal law protects his income, but one choice on the loan paperwork could haunt him well into his late…
 By Gerelyn Terzo 
 Published November 8, 2026, 7:35pm ET · 4 min read 
 The Full Benefits Desk desk. Editor: Gerelyn Terzo .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 Federal law bars lenders from discounting income because it is retirement benefits, so a 70-year-old's $3,000 Social Security check must count toward a motorcycle loan.
 Lenders can still deny loans based on credit history, debts, down payment and ability to repay, and Medicare premiums leave about $2,800 monthly.
 A $20,000 Harley loan at 9% costs about $415 monthly over five years or $322 over seven, which adds roughly $2,000 more interest.

 Harley-Davidson ( NYSE:HOG | HOG Price Prediction ) sold more than 25,000 new motorcycles at retail in North America in the third quarter of 2026. That was a 9% increase in units from a year earlier, as new models like the Super Glide and Deadwood brought riders into showrooms. Plenty of those buyers have gray in their beards.
 Consider a 70-year-old who wants one. His only regular income is a $3,000 monthly Social Security retirement benefit. He has picked out his bike, and now he’s at the financing desk wondering whether a lender can wave off that income just because it’s a government retirement payment.
 Federal law answers the income question clearly. Approval still depends on whether the payment fits his budget.
 Federal Law Makes the Lender Count His Benefit
 The Equal Credit Opportunity Act, enforced through a federal rule called Regulation B, prohibits lenders from dismissing Social Security retirement benefits simply because of where the income comes from. They must consider it alongside other sources of income when reviewing a loan application.
 Age gets similar protection. A lender generally can’t take an applicant’s age into account as long as he is able to sign a binding contract. A credit-scoring system may use age as a factor, but it cannot assign an elderly applicant a negative value for it.
 He can document his income with a benefit verification letter from his online Social Security account or bank statements showing the deposits. The lender may request additional documentation, but Social Security retirement benefits generally continue for life.
 Lenders Can Still Decline for Ordinary Reasons
 The same rule lets lenders consider how much income he receives and whether it will continue. They can’t discount his Social Security simply because it’s retirement income, but they can evaluate what he can afford. His credit history, existing debts, loan size, down payment and ability to repay still matter.
 If he’s enrolled in Medicare Part B and pays the standard $202.90 monthly premium in 2026, it’s usually deducted from his Social Security check. That leaves about $2,797 for housing, food, utilities, insurance and a motorcycle payment.
 What a $20,000 Harley Costs Him Every Month
 Here’s an example. He finances $20,000 at a 9% annual percentage rate (APR).
 Loan term 
 Monthly payment 
 Total interest paid 
 60 months 
 About $415 
 About $4,910 
 84 months 
 About $322 
 About $7,030 
 The five-year loan takes roughly 14% of his gross benefit. The seven-year loan feels easier each month, but he pays more interest and keeps making payments well into his late 70s.
 Run your own numbers, a different loan size, a lower rate, or extra payments, with this calculator:
 Inflation adjustments help unevenly. His benefit rose 2.8% in 2026, and an increase of 3.6% is set for 2027, while his loan payment remains the same. Social Security also paid 0% raises in 2009, 2010 and 2015. If the payment is tight today, future raises shouldn’t be what makes it work.
 Shopping around matters as much as the bike he picks. If he gets preapproved at a bank or credit union before going to the dealer, he has a rate to compare with the in-store offer from Harley-Davidson Financial Services, which made $786 million in retail loans last quarter. He should compare the APR and the total cost and get an insurance quote before signing. Lenders typically require full coverage on a financed bike, and that premium comes on top of the loan payment.
 A cheaper bike means a smaller loan. Harley plans to introduce the Sprint model and a returning Sportster 883 in the U.S. in the first half of 2027, with both aimed at buyers looking for a more affordable motorcycle.
 Two Decisions to Make Before He Signs
 First, figure out what the payment replaces. On a fixed income, every dollar that goes to a loan leaves less for everything else. If a surprise home or medical bill would force him to skip a payment, a bigger down payment or a cheaper model fixes that before it becomes a problem.
 Second, treat the loan term as the choice that’s hardest to undo. Missed payments can lead to repossession and damaged credit, and he may need that credit for a car or a home repair later. A shorter term costs less overall, as long as the monthly payment still leaves him some breathing room.
 His Social Security is real income, and the law makes sure the lender treats it that way. Whether the loan is a good idea for him comes down to his own savings, health and monthly bills, and those look different for every rider who walks into the showroom.
